ev.eth_fc_saint.mariam: {g:Gebre Mariam|Amete Mariam} – for the Virgin Mary
ev.eth_fc_saint.mariam.ok: The priest dipped you three times in the font and gave you a church name in honour of the Virgin Mary. A blue matab cord was tied round your neck.
ev.eth_fc_saint.giyorgis.ok: You were named for Saint George, the horseman who slew the dragon. "This one will be brave," said the priest, tying the matab round your neck.
ev.eth_fc_saint.mikael: {g:Haile Mikael|Wolete Mikael} – for the Archangel Michael
ev.eth_fc_saint.mikael.ok: The Archangel Michael leads the heavenly host and guards souls. The priest gave you his name and promised you a mighty protector.
ev.eth_fc_saint.title: The baptismal name
ev.eth_fc_saint.text: You are baptised on the {g:fortieth|eightieth} day, and the priest asks what church name to give you – to whom you shall belong. You can be placed under the mantle of the Virgin Mary, under the hand of Saint George, or under the wing of the Archangel Michael. This name will be used in church and at home, and the saint will be your protector for life.
ev.eth_fc_saint.note: Ethiopian Christians received at baptism – boys on the 40th day, girls on the 80th – a second, church name: Gebre Mariam ("servant of Mary"), Wolde Giyorgis ("son of George"), Haile Mikael ("power of Michael"). Each day of the month is dedicated to a saint: the 12th to Michael, the 21st to Mary, the 23rd to George. On these days the faithful gather in fellowships, mahber, taking turns to host one another.
ev.eth_fc_saint_mahber.title: Mary's fellowship
ev.eth_fc_saint_mahber.text: On the twenty-first of the month the neighbours of the Virgin Mary's fellowship gathered, as always, in one of their houses – and this time they invited you: "You've been Mary's since the font." You carried round bread and tella, listened to the prayers and the old men's stories, and left knowing that next time it would be your house's turn to host.
ev.eth_fc_saint_hyena.title: In George's name
ev.eth_fc_saint_hyena.text: Towards evening a hyena slunk out of the bushes towards your herd. No grown-ups were near, and you gripped your staff, shouted "Giyorgis!" and walked straight at it. The hyena backed off and vanished, and that evening the whole village said it was no accident you were named for the warrior saint.
ev.eth_fc_rist.feast.ok: For three days meat was roasted and tej poured in the yard, and the old men, stroking their beards, recited your ancestors back seven generations. Your father sat beaming, though the granary was noticeably emptier.
ev.eth_fc_rist.modest.ok: Only the neighbours were invited; bread was baked and tella brewed. A warm, cheap evening – though your father was thoughtful all night.
ev.eth_fc_rist.title: A feast for the elders
ev.eth_fc_rist.text: Your father wants to throw a great feast at your christening and invite the old men of the whole district: let them all see and remember whose lineage you are. On that, he says, depends whether you will ever get your share of the family land – the rist. The feast will cost sacks of teff and jars of honey tej, and your mother waves it away: everyone knows whose child it is anyway.
ev.eth_fc_rist.note: Rist was a hereditary right to a share of land, descending from the founder of a lineage through both the male and the female line. It had to be proved by reciting one's ancestors before elders and judges, and rist lawsuits dragged on for years. Cases were often heard in the open air, in the shade of a great tree.
ev.eth_fc_rist_won.title: The elders remember
ev.eth_fc_rist_won.text: Distant kin laid claim to your family's share of the rist: your line, they said, had nothing to do with that land. At the hearing under the old sycamore a grey-haired man stood up: "I drank tej at this child's christening and heard the ancestors recited." Others stood after him, and the land stayed with your family – and your share with you.
ev.eth_fc_rist_lost.title: The rist lawsuit
ev.eth_fc_rist_lost.text: Distant kin laid claim to your family's share of the rist, and at the hearing under the sycamore none of the old men could recall your ancestors beyond your grandfather. The judge divided the land, and part of it went to strangers. Your father walked out of the circle without a word – and you understood what he had been thinking at your christening.
